column4: The Lord names one straight path (صِرَاطِي) and forbids the plural paths (السُّبُل) that divide its walkers.
The Prophet is commanded to say that his Lord guided him to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), a steadfast religion (دِينًا قِيَمًا).
Moses, traveling toward Midian, asks God to guide him to the middle of the way (سَوَاءَ السَّبِيل), matching the path's center and the lost traveler's prayer.
Mountains, rivers, and roads (سُبُلًا) are placed on earth so people may find their way (تَهْتَدُونَ).
Wayfinding marks (عَلَامَاتٍ) and stars (النَّجْم) give travelers signs by which to find direction (يَهْتَدُونَ).
God spreads the earth as a cradle and makes roads (سُبُلًا) through it so people may be guided (تَهْتَدُوا).
God sets firm mountains and makes broad passes (فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا) through the earth so people may find their way.
The earth is made a resting place with roads (سُبُلًا) running through it for travelers to be guided.
The earth is spread out with broad roads (فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا) for people to travel along.
God measures travel between settled towns (قَدَّرْنَا فِيهَا السَّيْرَ), making a network of known stages through the landscape.
The travelers ask for longer distances (بَاعِدْ بَيْنَ أَسْفَارِنَا) and are scattered, turning a safe route into a judgment on a community.
A bewildered person in open country (حَيْرَانَ) is called toward guidance (الْهُدَى) by companions waiting on the path.
God finds the Prophet ضَالًّا and guides him (فَهَدَىٰ); this can mean one who had not found the way, as well as one astray.
Iblis vows to sit in ambush on God's straight path (صِرَاطَكَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ), making the traveled route contested ground.
Iblis describes attacking from every direction—front, back, right, and left—around the straight route.
The criminals are ordered to separate (امْتَازُوا) before the route of worship and the route of error are named.
The covenant forbids worshipping Satan (اعْبُدُوا الشَّيْطَانَ), the rival guide who diverts people from the straight way.
God says to worship Him (اعْبُدُونِي): this is the straight path (صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ), joining service to the route itself.
Satan has led (أَضَلَّ) many people astray from that path, making the counter-route visible.
The destination of the diverted route is identified as the Hell they were promised (تُوعَدُونَ).
They are told to enter and burn in that destination (اصْلَوْهَا), completing the way from misguidance to its end.
Jesus says God is his Lord and theirs, so worship Him; this is a straight path (صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ).
Jesus again joins worship of God (اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ) to the straight way (صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ).
Jesus repeats that worship of God is the straight path (صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ), a parallel witness to the Fatiha's worship-path image.
The condemned are to be guided (فَاهْدُوهُمْ) to the path of Hell (صِرَاطِ الْجَحِيم), where guidance leads to the contrary destination.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), answering the question of direction in the qibla passage.
The community is made a middle nation (أُمَّةً وَسَطًا), with its direction tested through following the Messenger.
God brings believers from darkness into light, while false patrons lead others back into darkness: two opposed routes and guides.
Obedience to God and the Messenger is followed by guidance to a straight path (صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا), immediately before the description of the favored people.
Those who obey God and the Messenger join the prophets, truthful, martyrs, and righteous whom God favored (أَنْعَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ), naming the community whose path is sought.
One who opposes the Messenger and follows a way other than the believers' (سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ) is left to that chosen route.
Those who hold fast to God are guided to Him on a straight path (صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا).
Keeping the covenant leads to pardon and gardens; disbelief after it is straying from the middle of the way (سَوَاءَ السَّبِيل).
The Messenger brings light and a clarifying Book from God, preparing the next verse's account of guidance out of darkness.
The Book guides those seeking God's approval to paths of peace (سُبُلَ السَّلَام), brings them from darkness to light, and guides them to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
Each community is given a law and a way (شِرْعَةً وَمِنْهَاجًا); the passage preserves plurality while telling them to race in good deeds.
Some are placed on a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), while others are left in layered darkness, a direct split between finding and losing the way.
The chosen forebears and descendants are guided to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), a line of favored predecessors.
God calls this direction His guidance (هُدَى اللَّهِ) and commands the Prophet to follow the guided predecessors.
Stars (النُّجُوم) orient travelers in land and sea at night; they are signs for people who know how to read them.
The constricted chest of one turned away is likened to climbing into the sky, a bodily contrast before the Lord's straight path is named.
The Lord calls this straight path (صِرَاطُ رَبِّكَ مُسْتَقِيمًا) and says it is made clear for those who remember.
The command to weigh with a just balance (الْمِيزَانَ بِالْقِسْطِ) stands among the teachings immediately before the one-path instruction.
The Book given to Moses is a completion, clarification, guidance, and mercy, continuing the preceding instruction about God's path.
The people are forbidden to sit on every road (بِكُلِّ صِرَاطٍ) to threaten travelers and bar them from God's way (سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ).
Those who turn arrogant from God's signs refuse the path of right guidance (سَبِيلَ الرُّشْد) and choose the path of error (سَبِيلَ الْغَيِّ).
God calls people to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
The passage asks who guides to the truth (يَهْدِي إِلَى الْحَقِّ) and who is more worthy to be followed, testing the guide as well as the route.
Hud says his Lord is on a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), presenting divine governance as the unwavering route.
Pharaoh will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection to the Fire (فَأَوْرَدَهُمُ النَّارَ), a false guide taking a community to ruin.
The Prophet calls to God with insight and declares, “This is my way” (سَبِيلِي), along with whoever follows him.
The Book brings people from darkness to light by their Lord's leave, onto the path of the Mighty and Praiseworthy (صِرَاطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ).
The good word is likened to a tree with a firm root (أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ) and branches in the sky, an image of a practice that holds and bears fruit.
The rooted tree gives its fruit at every season (كُلَّ حِينٍ), like a way sustained through repeated acts.
The evil word is an uprooted tree with no stability (اجْتُثَّتْ مِن فَوْقِ الْأَرْضِ مَا لَهَا مِن قَرَارٍ), the opposite of a path worn firm by faithful walkers.
God makes believers firm with the steadfast word (الْقَوْلِ الثَّابِتِ) in this life and the next, keeping them on their ground.
Iblis vows to mislead all people (لَأُغْوِيَنَّهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ), naming the rival guide's aim.
Iblis admits that God's sincere servants are outside his power, preserving a community that does not take his route.
God answers, “This is a straight path to Me” (صِرَاطٌ عَلَيَّ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ), placing the route under divine claim.
God's servants are beyond Iblis's authority except those who follow the deviants (الْغَاوِينَ), marking the boundary between routes.
The straight direction of the way (قَصْدُ السَّبِيل) belongs to God, while some routes swerve (جَائِر); this preserves both destination and deviation.
Every community receives a messenger calling it to worship God and shun false gods; some are guided and others deserve error.
Abraham is called a whole community (أُمَّةً) in himself, devoted and upright, a single forerunner whose life becomes a way to follow.
Abraham is grateful for blessings and is guided to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), explicitly tying favor to the exemplary route.
The Qur'an guides to what is most upright (أَقْوَمُ), naming revelation as the sign that straightens a walk.
Every people is called with its leader (بِإِمَامِهِمْ), showing a community's way and its guide brought into judgment.
Whoever is blind to guidance here will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way (أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا).
Moses asks to follow the servant of God so he may learn right guidance (رُشْدًا), making the learner seek a guide ahead of him.
Abraham invites his father to follow him and says God will guide him to a straight path (صِرَاطًا سَوِيًّا).
The prophets are those God guided and favored; when the signs are recited they fall in prostration, exemplars along the path.
Later successors neglect prayer and follow desires (اتَّبَعُوا الشَّهَوَات), meeting ruin instead of the prophets' way.
Moses says God gave each thing its form and then guided it (هَدَىٰ), extending wayfinding to every creature's fitting course.
People are told to eat and pasture their cattle in the earth's provision; signs in the land continue the road scene.
People come from earth, return to it, and are brought out again, placing the traveled life inside a larger passage.
Pharaoh led his people astray (أَضَلَّ قَوْمَهُ) and did not guide them (وَمَا هَدَىٰ), the false herdsman of a community.
Whoever follows God's guidance will not go astray or be wretched, while turning from the reminder has the contrary end.
Turning away from God's reminder brings a constricted life and blindness on the Day of Resurrection, the lost traveler's outcome.
The closing challenge asks which group is more guided and whose way is more right (أَهْدَىٰ سَبِيلًا), leaving the route open to judgment.
Abraham's family is made leaders guiding by God's command (أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا), a community that leads ahead.
The arrogant turns aside to mislead others from God's way (لِيُضِلَّ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّه), the counter-motion to guidance.
Believers are guided to good speech and to the path of the Praiseworthy (صِرَاطِ الْحَمِيد).
Some bar people from God's way and from the Sacred Mosque (يَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ), placing an obstruction on both route and destination.
Those given knowledge know revelation is truth from their Lord, and God guides believers to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
The Prophet says he calls people to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), making the call itself a path forward.
Those who do not believe in the Hereafter turn away from the path (الصِّرَاطِ), showing how a destination shapes direction.
Clear signs are sent, and God guides whom He wills to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
The Prophet asks no wage except that a person may take a way to his Lord (سَبِيلًا), naming the response as a chosen route.
Moses is told to strike the sea; it parts into a dry path (طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا) for his people to cross.
The Queen's people are barred from God's way (فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيل), their worship misdirected by Satan's beautification.
God guides people through land and sea darkness and sends winds as good news; the question is who makes a traveler find the way.
Pharaoh's chiefs are made leaders calling to the Fire (أَئِمَّةً يَدْعُونَ إِلَى النَّار), a guide-community turned toward ruin.
Following desire without God's guidance is called greater error (أَضَلُّ), exposing an attractive but unmarked route.
Those who strive for God are guided to His many ways (سُبُلَنَا), while God remains with those who do good.
The upright religion (الدِّينُ الْقَيِّم) is aligned with the human nature God created, naming a way of life that does not bend from its fit.
Leaders who guide by God's command (أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا) emerge through patience and certainty.
People say they followed their chiefs and were turned away from the way (السَّبِيلَا), preserving the danger of walking behind the wrong guide.
Those given knowledge see revelation as truth that guides to the path of the Mighty and Praiseworthy (صِرَاطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيد).
The Prophet says misguidance harms himself and guidance comes through what his Lord reveals, keeping wayfinding dependent on revelation.
The inheritors of the Book divide into those who wrong themselves, those moderate, and those who race ahead in good, preserving parallel walks within one inheritance.
The Qur'an says the Messenger is on a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), the way embodied by the guide.
A man comes running from the far side of the city and urges people to follow messengers who ask no wage and are rightly guided (مُهْتَدُونَ).
Abraham says he is going to his Lord and expects Him to guide him (سَيَهْدِينِ), a traveler trusting the guide ahead.
Moses and Aaron are guided to the straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), continuing the prophets' line of guides.
The disputants ask David to guide them to the middle of the way (سَوَاءِ الصِّرَاط), bringing the path's center into the Qur'an's own language.
David is told to judge with truth and not follow desire lest it lead him astray from God's way (سَبِيلِ اللَّه).
The guided are those who listen and follow the best of what they hear (فَيَتَّبِعُونَ أَحْسَنَهُ), discerning which voice to walk behind.
An opened heart for Islam is a light from the Lord; a hardened heart is in manifest error, contrasting readiness to receive the route.
The best teaching is sent down as a repeated Book; skins and hearts soften to God's reminder, which is His guidance (هُدَى اللَّه).
Whoever God guides cannot be led astray (مَن يَهْدِ اللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُ مِن مُّضِلٍّ), securing the guide's authority.
The Book is sent with truth for people; whoever accepts guidance does so for himself and whoever strays bears his own loss.
Disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell, where its gates open; the wrong route has a collective destination.
Those mindful of God are led in groups to the Garden; the two processions show opposing roads and ends.
Pharaoh claims, “I guide you only to the way of right conduct” (سَبِيلَ الرَّشَاد), though he leads toward ruin.
The believing man answers with the same words—follow me and I will guide you to the way of right conduct (سَبِيلَ الرَّشَاد)—contesting Pharaoh's false direction.
The believer says, “Why do I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?” making rival calls into opposed roads.
The false object of worship cannot answer a call; the return is to God and transgressors end in the Fire.
Thamud are shown guidance, yet choose blindness over it (اسْتَحَبُّوا الْعَمَىٰ عَلَى الْهُدَى), an explicit refusal of the marked way.
The same religion is prescribed to Noah and later messengers; people are told to establish it and not divide over it.
Ships on the sea are likened to mountains (كَالْأَعْلَامِ), the root's mountain-markers rising as navigational signs.
Revelation is made a light by which people guide others, and the Prophet is told that he guides to a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
People defend inherited religion by saying they found their fathers on a community (أُمَّةٍ) and follow their traces (آثَارِهِمْ), a path by habit rather than guidance.
The same inherited-trace argument is repeated by earlier communities whenever a warner comes, showing how an old track can resist a guide.
The messenger asks whether he has brought better guidance than the ancestral way; they insist on following their fathers.
Those turned from God's reminder by Satan think they are rightly guided (يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ), though he bars them from the path (السَّبِيل).
The Prophet is told to hold fast to what is revealed because he is on a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
The passage says not to doubt and to follow God; this is a straight path (صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ), while preserving the disputed reading around Jesus and the Hour.
Jesus comes with clear proofs and commands fear of God and obedience, the lead-in to his straight-path statement.
The groups differ among themselves after Jesus' clear statement, turning the one straight way into dispute.
The Prophet is set upon a revealed way of the matter (شَرِيعَةٍ) and commanded to follow it, not the desires of the ignorant.
The jinn say the revealed Book guides to truth and a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), making them fellow travelers who recognize the sign.
Those already guided are given increased guidance (زَادَهُمْ هُدًى), so the path deepens through continued attention.
Those who disbelieve and bar others from God's way (صَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّه) obstruct the route for other walkers.
The Prophet is promised guidance to a straight path (صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا), joined to forgiveness and divine favor.
Faith is made beloved and disbelief hateful to the believers, and the verse names them as rightly guided (الرَّاشِدُون).
That rightly guided state is described as grace and favor from God (فَضْلًا وَنِعْمَةً), linking the community to bestowed favor.
The believers' light runs ahead of them and at their right (نُورُهُم يَسْعَىٰ بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ), like a sign lighting the road to the Garden.
God gives believers a light by which they walk (نُورًا تَمْشُونَ بِهِ), making guidance visible underfoot.
The verse contrasts one who walks face down with one who walks upright on a straight path (سَوِيًّا عَلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ).
God shows the human being the way (هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيل), leaving him grateful or ungrateful, two responses after direction is made clear.
God guides the human to two conspicuous heights or ways (النَّجْدَيْن), placing a choice between routes before him.
The hard ascent (الْعَقَبَة) is not taken, introducing the difficult but fitting route of service.
The steep ascent is explained as a demanding passage, not a flat or effortless walk.
Freeing a slave is the first act on the steep path (فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ).
Feeding on a day of hunger continues the difficult route of mercy.
The hungry one is an orphan near of kin, giving the route a concrete vulnerable traveler.
The route reaches a poor person in dust (مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ).
Those who take it join faith to mutual patience and mercy (تَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْمَرْحَمَةِ).
The people of the right are the community who pass along that steep route (أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ).
The one who gives and is mindful begins a repeated course of action that God will make easy toward ease (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ).
Affirming the best (صَدَّقَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ) is the conviction that accompanies the easy route.
God makes the generous person's way easy toward ease (لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), showing habit as ground made traversable.
The one who withholds and feels self-sufficient begins the contrary course.
Denying the best (كَذَّبَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ) marks the opposite belief and direction.
God makes that person's way easy toward hardship (لِلْعُسْرَىٰ), preserving the contrary reading of a path made easy in the wrong direction.
Guidance itself rests with God (إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ), the ground of the two routes just described.
People are commanded to worship God with sincere devotion, as an upright religion (الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمَة), joining sustained service to the straight way.
Those who trade guidance for error make a losing exchange (اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلَالَةَ بِالْهُدَى), choosing the wrong route after seeing both.
People refuse revelation and follow inherited footsteps instead (نَتَّبِعُ مَا أَلْفَيْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَاءَنَا), even when those before them lacked guidance.
Humanity begins as one community, then disputes; prophets and Scripture guide the people to truth (يَهْدِي اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا), preserving unity and divergence.
The prayer asks God not to let hearts deviate after guidance (لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا), a plea to stay on the route.
The community is told to hold fast together to God's rope and not divide (وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا), keeping many walkers on one shared course.
A community is to call others to good, command right, and forbid wrong, acting as guides along the way.
Had the people obeyed the instruction to leave home or fight, it would have been better and firmer for them; steadfastness follows submission.
Obedience would bring a great reward from God, continuing the preceding promise of a firm route.
Satan curses himself and claims he will take a share of God's servants, presenting a rival master for people to follow.
Satan promises to command his followers to alter God's creation; taking him as patron is named a clear loss.
People are warned against desires of those who went astray, misled many, and left the middle of the way (سَوَاءَ السَّبِيل).
The Prophet is told to follow the guidance (هُدَاهُم) of the earlier prophets, an explicit line of predecessors.
Following most people would lead away from God's way (سَبِيلِ اللَّه), since they follow conjecture rather than a marked route.
One group is guided and another earns error; some take devils as allies while thinking themselves guided.
Those who follow the Messenger find him described in earlier scripture and follow the light sent with him.
Whom God guides is truly guided, and whom He leaves astray are the losers, preserving both readings of the journey.
Believers are called to what gives them life when God and the Messenger call them, a response to the guide's summons.
The first forerunners among emigrants and helpers, and those who follow them well, form a favored succession of walkers.
Some from each community are to learn religion and return to warn their people, keeping guidance moving from one group to the next.
Believers are guided by their faith (يَهْدِيهِمْ رَبُّهُم بِإِيمَانِهِمْ) toward gardens beneath which rivers flow.
Moses and Aaron are told to remain upright (فَاسْتَقِيمَا) and not follow the way of those who do not know.
The Prophet says truth has come from the Lord; whoever accepts guidance does so for himself and whoever strays bears his own loss.
The Prophet and those with him are commanded to remain steadfast (فَاسْتَقِمْ) as ordered, a daily continuation on the straight way.
They are told not to incline toward wrongdoers, lest the Fire touch them, guarding the course from a harmful pull.
Every people has a guide (هَادٍ), distinguishing the one who warns from the guide who leads ahead.
Messengers speak in their people's language to make the message clear; God guides or leaves astray whom He wills.
People set rivals up to lead others away from God's way (لِيُضِلُّوا عَن سَبِيلِهِ), redirecting walkers from their Lord.
Ships travel through the sea and people seek provision from it, extending the created landscape around the roads and stars.
God could make humanity one community but lets some stray and guides others; every group is answerable for its practiced course.
Whoever is guided benefits himself, and no bearer carries another's burden, locating responsibility in each walker's steps.
One who seeks the Hereafter and strives as a believer has effort acknowledged, preserving the route chosen toward the lasting home.
The sleepers' cave is described by the sun's course; the verse then says whom God guides is rightly guided and whom He leaves astray has no protecting guide.
Moses says he will continue traveling until he reaches the meeting of the seas, setting out to seek knowledge.
The fish slips into the sea by a remarkable passage (سَرَبًا), a sign at the travelers' meeting place.
Moses asks for their meal after the journey has worn them out (نَصَبًا), a bodily detail of the path.
The servant explains how the fish took its way into the sea (اتَّخَذَ سَبِيلَهُ), making a sign into a direction.
Moses recognizes the sign as what they were seeking, and they retrace their steps (فَارْتَدَّا عَلَىٰ آثَارِهِمَا).
They find a servant whom God gave mercy and taught knowledge, the guide at the end of their search.
The servant warns Moses he will not be able to remain patient with him, the trial of following a guide whose path is not yet understood.
Moses is told he cannot encompass the servant's knowledge, a limit on the traveler's sight.
Moses promises patience and obedience, the learner's commitment to follow the guide.
The servant sets a condition: do not ask until he explains, ordering the learner's steps.
The greatest losers are those whose effort went astray while they thought they were doing good (ضَلَّ سَعْيُهُمْ), a path misread from within.
God increases guidance for those already guided (زَادَهُمُ اللَّهُ هُدًى), and enduring good works are better in reward.
Isaac and Jacob are given to Abraham, setting up the family of leaders who guide by God's command in the next verse.
Every messenger is told that there is no god but God, so worship Him alone, a repeated foundation of the prophets' route.
Every community has a rite to follow (مَنسَكًا هُمْ نَاسِكُوهُ), preserving differences in practice while calling the Prophet to his Lord.
God guides to His light whom He wills; the parable of the lamp makes direction visible in darkness.
Obeying God and the Messenger is followed by guidance (تَهْتَدُوا), joining listening to walking rightly.
Every prophet faces enemies among criminals, while God is enough as guide (هَادِيًا) and helper.
The servants of the Merciful walk gently upon earth (يَمْشُونَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ هَوْنًا), making their manner of walking an ethical sign.
The faithful pray to be made leaders for the mindful (إِمَامًا), asking to become exemplars others can follow.
People are told to travel the land and see the traces and end of earlier communities, reading the consequences left along the way.
Travel through the land and see how earlier peoples ended, including the traces of their choices.
Even when parents call to association, one must not obey but should follow the way of those who turn to God (سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّ).
The instruction to be moderate in walking (وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ) and lower one's voice gives the path a measured gait.
People are asked to travel through the land and see the end of those before them, whose greater power did not save them.
Travelers are asked to inspect the remains and fate of earlier peoples, reading the history written along the earth.
The same call to travel and see the end of earlier peoples turns the land into evidence for a walker's judgment.
The same Lord created the heavens and earth, the setting for the roads and traveling signs in the next verses.
Rain revives dead earth after the roads are named; the passage moves from the traveler’s route to the sign of return.
One who makes desire his god is left to hearing and sight sealed, a self-directed route that mistakes appetite for a guide.
People are told to travel the land and see the fate of those before them, the route bearing visible traces of prior choices.
The Companions' mark of prostration and likeness to a seed that strengthens and thickens portray a community growing through following.
Humans and jinn are created to worship God (لِيَعْبُدُونِ), giving the path of service a stated purpose.
Satan's party forgets God and becomes the losing party, a community following a rival guide.
Those with faith written in their hearts are God's party, set against Satan's party as two loyalties and destinations.
The emigrants who left homes for God's favor and help form the first community of the path.
The Helpers love those who migrated and prefer them over themselves, preserving the conduct of a community that receives later walkers.
Believers are told to look at what they have sent ahead for tomorrow (قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ), making each day's steps matter at the destination.
Those who forget God forget themselves; they are the rebellious, losing their orientation and their own way.
Abraham and those with him are presented as a model in disavowing false worship and turning to God, though the passage preserves the limits of that example.
God creates and proportions (خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ), making the world fit before the next verse says He determines and guides.
God determines and then guides (قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ), joining measured form to an assigned direction.
Those who disbelieve the signs are people of the left, the contrary community to those who complete the steep ascent.
Fire closes over the people of the left, showing the far end of their chosen course.
The soul is proportioned (سَوَّاهَا), recalling a made-fit form before its moral directions are described.
The soul is shown its wickedness and its mindfulness (فُجُورَهَا وَتَقْوَاهَا), the inward signs of two possible routes.
The one who purifies the soul succeeds (أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا), a practiced course bearing its result.
The one who buries the soul fails (خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا), preserving the contrary outcome.
Night covers and day shines, a recurring sign of alternation that frames the two courses in the following oath.
The bright day is paired with the covered night before the passage distinguishes different human striving.
The creation of male and female precedes the statement that people's efforts and paths differ.
Human striving goes in different directions (إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ), preparing the opposed easy and hard routes.
When the miser falls, his wealth will not save him, the consequence of the hardship-bound course.
The Hereafter and this life belong to God, framing the two courses by their final destination.
Time is sworn by as it passes, measuring the repeated ground on which the path is walked.
Human beings are in loss except for the community of faith and good work, those who exchange truth and patience.
Mutual counsel in truth and patience makes steadfast companions on the way rather than isolated walkers.
The instruction to enter houses by their doors (وَأْتُوا الْبُيُوتَ مِنْ أَبْوَابِهَا) makes finding the right entrance a small image of reaching the home by its proper way.
Travel through the land and see the end of those who denied the signs, treating the earth as a record of prior travelers.
The hearers are asked whether they have traveled the land and seen the end of earlier peoples, reading the path through its traces.
The Prophet is told to stay with those who call their Lord morning and evening and not follow a heedless heart's desire, a daily community of walkers.
After finishing his term, Moses travels with his family and sees a fire from the mountain's side, continuing the journey begun toward Midian.
Whoever turns away from the Reminder is assigned a devil as companion, who then bars him from the path in the next verse.
God makes the human's way easy (ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ), a bodily path from origin into life.
Those who break God's covenant and sever what He commanded to be joined are named losers, the communal fragmentation opposed to a worn shared path.
Believers are told to enter submission wholly and not follow Satan's footsteps (خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَان), a contrary trail laid for walkers.
People prefer the inherited track (مَا أَلْفَيْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَاءَنَا) over what God revealed, even when their fathers knew no guidance.
People are forbidden to follow Satan's footsteps (خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَان), a repeated trail leading away from God's route.
Satan and his tribe see humans while humans do not see them; the warning not to follow Satan's footsteps preserves the hidden ambush on the path.
Those who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter turn others away from God's way (يَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّه), making desire an obstruction.
Iblis and his descendants are taken as allies instead of God, a choice of the rival company that once refused the command.
Believers are told not to follow Satan's footsteps (خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَان), whose trail commands indecency and wrong.
Those who follow desire without knowledge are left astray; no one can guide the person God leaves in error.
Those who turn back after guidance are led by Satan and given false hopes, abandoning the route after it was shown.
The mindful are already described as being upon guidance from their Lord (هُدًى), the grounded state of those who find the way.
God guides many by a parable and leaves many astray through it; only the defiantly disobedient are left to their error.
God promises that when guidance (هُدًى) comes from Him, whoever follows it will have no fear or grief.
Those who reject the signs and deny them are companions of the Fire, the contrary end to following guidance.
Whoever rejects false gods and believes in God has grasped the firm handhold (الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ) that cannot break, an image of a secure route.
Believers are told to fear God as He deserves and remain wholly submitted until death, a sustained course of devotion.
Some given a share of Scripture buy error and want others to stray from the way (السَّبِيل), choosing a route and inviting others onto it.
The favor described for those who obey God and the Messenger is bounty from God, completing the account of the favored company.
Believers must stand firm for justice (كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ) and not let hatred turn them aside; justice is nearer to mindfulness.
Believers are told to seek a means of approach to God (الْوَسِيلَةَ) and strive in His way, naming the route of nearness.
This blessed Book is sent down so people may follow it (فَاتَّبِعُوهُ) and be mindful, continuing the path stated in the preceding verse.
The wrongdoers bar people from God's way (سَبِيلِ اللَّه) and seek to make it crooked, while denying the Hereafter.
The Prophet is told to announce his universal mission and command belief in God and following him (فَاتَّبِعُوهُ) so people may be guided.
Among Moses's people is a community that guides by truth (يَهْدُونَ بِالْحَقِّ) and judges justly, a faithful group within a divided people.
Among God's creation is a community that guides by truth (يَهْدُونَ بِالْحَقِّ) and acts justly, preserving the presence of a rightly directed company.
People who prefer family, wealth, trade, and homes over God, His Messenger, and striving in His way are warned of a rival attachment that displaces the path.
Believing men and women are allies who command right, establish prayer, and obey God and His Messenger; God will show them mercy.
The believing community is characterized by repentance, worship, praise, devotion, command of right, and guarding God's limits, a practiced way of life.
Some ask for a sign, but God leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back (مَنْ أَنَابَ), linking return to finding the way.
The messengers ask why they would not rely on God when He has guided them to their ways (سُبُلَنَا), and promise patience on that course.
Night, day, sun, moon, and stars are made subject to human use as signs for people who reason, complementing the landscape's markers.
The parable contrasts a powerless owned servant (عَبْدًا مَّمْلُوكًا) with one who spends from good provision, preparing the next verse's contrast with a just man on a straight path.
The just man commands equity and is upon a straight path (صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ), while the mute servant is a burden to his master.
The Book is sent as clarification, guidance (هُدًى), mercy, and good news for those who submit, a guide for every community.
The Prophet is told to follow Abraham's religion (مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ), a straight way linked to the exemplary guide just described.
Whom God guides is rightly guided, and whom He leaves astray has no protector; they are gathered blind, mute, and deaf.
God is forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does right, and then remains guided (اهْتَدَىٰ), depicting a return to the path.
Believers are told to bow, prostrate, worship their Lord, and do good, the embodied service immediately before the command to hold fast to Him.
Believers are told to strive for God, follow Abraham's religion, hold fast to Him, and keep prayer; He is their patron and the best patron.
On the Day of Gathering, the worshipped are asked whether they led God's servants astray or whether the servants themselves strayed from the way (ضَلُّوا السَّبِيل).
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are the worst in position and furthest astray from the way (أَضَلُّ سَبِيلًا).
Moses says his Lord is with him and will guide him (سَيَهْدِينِ) as the sea and pursuing army close in.
Abraham says his Lord created him and guides him (يَهْدِينِ), an exemplary wayfinder's confession.
God makes the earth a stable dwelling, sets rivers and mountains within it, and separates the seas, the landscape around the traveler's way.
The Prophet cannot guide the blind out of their error (ضَلَالَتِهِمْ); only those who believe in God's signs will hear.
At the water of Midian, Moses finds two women holding back their flock while shepherds water theirs, continuing his journey toward a new home.
Moses waters the women's flock, withdraws to shade, and asks God for any good provision, a traveler acting generously while seeking refuge.
One of the women comes walking modestly to invite Moses to meet her father, extending the route from the well to a household.
The daughter describes Moses as strong and trustworthy (الْقَوِيُّ الْأَمِينُ), the qualities of a dependable guide and keeper.
Moses is offered a household and a period of service, turning the traveler's arrival into an enduring place in a community.
Moses confirms the agreed term, closing the journey sequence with a fulfilled pledge.
The Prophet cannot guide whom he loves; God guides whom He wills and knows best those ready to be guided.
Ad and Thamud are led astray by Satan after he beautifies their deeds and bars them from the way (السَّبِيل), though they had insight.
God's earth is spacious, so believers are told to worship Him alone wherever they are (فَإِيَّايَ فَاعْبُدُونِ), carrying service along the road.
The Prophet cannot guide the blind from their error (ضَلَالَتِهِمْ); only those who believe the signs will hear and submit.
The Qur'an is guidance (هُدًى) and mercy for those who do good, beginning the portrait of people who are on their Lord's direction.
They establish prayer, give alms, and are certain of the Hereafter, practices that fill out the guided life described next.
Such people are upon guidance from their Lord (هُدًى مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ) and are successful.
The Messenger is presented as a beautiful pattern (أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ) for those who hope in God and the Last Day, a model whose footsteps can be followed.
Believers are commanded to speak upright words (قَوْلًا سَدِيدًا), language that points straight rather than turning aside.
God promises to set their deeds right and forgive them, showing upright speech shaping the walk and its destination.
One whose evil deeds are made attractive and seem good is contrasted with the guided; God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.
God could erase people's sight so they would race toward the path (الصِّرَاط), yet would they truly see where they were going?
God could immobilize them where they stand so they could neither go forward nor return, the loss of all direction.
The wrongdoers, their companions, and what they worshipped are gathered before being directed to the path of Hell in the next verse.
People are told to turn to their Lord and submit before punishment comes, a return to the way before the final destination.
They are told to follow the best of what was revealed (اتَّبِعُوا أَحْسَنَ مَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكُم), a clear instruction for choosing the guide.
The people of the Garden praise God for fulfilling His promise and letting them inherit the land, the destination reached by the preceding procession.
On the Day of turning back, no one can protect the one God leaves astray (يُضْلِلِ اللَّهُ), and there is no guide for him.
Moses is given guidance (الْهُدَىٰ) and the Children of Israel inherit the Book, continuing the line of revealed guides.
The Book is guidance (هُدًى) and a reminder for people of understanding, making memory part of remaining on the way.
Those who say God is their Lord and remain steadfast (اسْتَقَامُوا) receive angels and the promise of the Garden.
Night, day, sun, and moon are signs; people are told to worship their Creator rather than the celestial markers that orient them.
The Prophet is told to stand firm as commanded (فَاسْتَقِمْ) and not follow their desires, a direct instruction to keep the straight course.
One whom God leaves astray has no protector after Him and, seeing punishment, asks to return to the world, when the route is already closed.
The straight path is identified as God's path (صِرَاطِ اللَّهِ), to whom belongs all in the heavens and earth.
Moses is commanded to travel by night with God's servants (فَأَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي), leading a community away from Pharaoh.
Those who say God is their Lord and then remain steadfast (اسْتَقَامُوا) have no fear or grief.
They are the companions of the Garden, abiding there as reward for what they did, completing the steadfast path's end.
Those who disbelieve and bar others from God's way (صَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ اللَّه) have their deeds made fruitless.
One who stands upon clear proof from the Lord is contrasted with one whose evil conduct is made attractive, exposing two different ways of seeing.
After promising victory, God says He will guide the believers to a straight path (صِرَاطًا مُّسْتَقِيمًا), placing success inside guidance.
God sends the Messenger with guidance (بِالْهُدَىٰ) and the religion of truth, preparing the portrait of his companions in the next verse.
The Garden is brought near to the mindful and is no longer far, the destination of the people who kept their course.
The Garden is promised to every returning and watchful person (أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ), describing the practiced character of its walkers.
Those who feared the Merciful unseen and came with a heart turned to Him are told to enter in peace.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who turns away from God's remembrance and desires only the nearer life.
That preference marks the limit of their knowledge; God knows best who has strayed from His way and who is guided.
Believers are told to race toward forgiveness and a Garden broad as heaven and earth, making the walk urgent and its destination clear.
When Moses's people deviate (زَاغُوا), God lets their hearts deviate; persistent turning away hardens the direction.
Whoever believes in God has the heart guided by Him (يَهْدِ قَلْبَهُ), bringing inward direction into the image.
For whoever is mindful of God, He makes a way out (مَخْرَجًا), an opening when the course is constrained.
God provides from an unexpected source and is enough for whoever relies on Him, sustaining the route He opens.
The earth is made tame (ذَلُولًا) for people to walk its slopes and eat its provision, closely echoing the image of a beaten, subdued road.
The Lord knows best who has strayed from His way (سَبِيلِهِ) and who is guided (الْمُهْتَدِينَ), judging the competing routes.
God makes the earth spread out (بِسَاطًا), immediately before describing its broad roads for travelers.
If people remain upright on the way (اسْتَقَامُوا عَلَى الطَّرِيقَةِ), God gives them abundant water, joining steadfastness to provision.
Believers are told to recite what is easy, keep prayer, give alms, and send good ahead to find it with God, the repeated practices of a sustained path.
The Qur'an is a reminder, and whoever wills may take a way to his Lord (اتَّخَذَ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِ سَبِيلًا).
Human willing remains under God's will, preserving divine guidance alongside the traveler's choice.
The one who transgresses (طَغَىٰ) begins the contrary course described in the next verses.
Preferring the nearer life (آثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا) makes the path turn away from the lasting home.
Hell is the destination of that preference (فَإِنَّ الْجَحِيمَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ).
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire takes the opposing route.
The Garden is the home of that restrained soul (فَإِنَّ الْجَنَّةَ هِيَ الْمَأْوَىٰ), the other destination.
The question “Where are you going?” (فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ) turns the hearer toward the direction of the Qur'an's reminder.
The Qur'an is a reminder for all worlds, making the call to choose a way universal.
Whoever wills among you may take a straight way (أَن يَسْتَقِيمَ), the explicit direction behind the question.
People do not will except as God wills, holding human choice and divine guidance together.
The human being toils toward his Lord (كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا) and will meet Him, a life-long walk to a destination.
People are told they will move from stage to stage (طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ), marking life as passage through successive conditions.
The one who purifies himself (تَزَكَّىٰ) succeeds, an active course that bears good fruit.
He remembers his Lord's name and prays, giving the purified path its repeated practice.
People prefer the nearer life (تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا), choosing the short road over what lasts.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting (خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ), naming the destination that endures.
God gives the human being two eyes, bodily signs that precede the verse about two conspicuous paths.
The tongue and lips make speech possible, another gift before the way between good and evil is shown.
The Fire is warned of as the blazing destination (نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ) of the contrary course.
Only the most wretched (الْأَشْقَى) enters that fire, identifying the one who rejects the way.
The one who denies truth and turns away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ) is marked by refusal of the guidance.
The most mindful is kept far from the Fire (وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا الْأَتْقَى), the saved walker's contrary end.
He gives from his wealth to purify himself (يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ يَتَزَكَّىٰ), continuing the giving course of the opening verses.
His giving is not payment for a favor owed to anyone, preserving sincerity in the route.
He gives only seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High (ابْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ الْأَعْلَىٰ).
He will be satisfied (وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ), the promised end of the purified course.
God found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter, one of the favors surrounding the lost-and-guided verse.
God found the Prophet in need and enriched him, another bestowal (أَغْنَىٰ) beside the guidance of verse 7.
The Prophet is commanded not to oppress the orphan, turning received favor into care for another traveler.
He is told not to repel the one who asks, a concrete practice for those who have received guidance.
He is told to proclaim the favor of his Lord (بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ), explicitly recalling the root in “those You favored.”
When one task is finished, the Prophet is told to strive on (فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَانصَبْ), continuing the work without stopping on the road.
He is told to turn his desire toward his Lord (وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَارْغَب), fixing the route's destination.
Those who believe and do good are called the best of creation (خَيْرُ الْبَرِيَّةِ), the community walking the upright religion.
Their reward is gardens of lasting residence and God's pleasure, the end of the path of worship and sincerity.
Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it, making every small step visible at judgment.
Whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it too, preserving accountability for every contrary step.
The closing distinction “you have your religion and I have mine” (لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِيَ دِينِ) preserves divergent commitments and ways of life.
People enter God's religion in crowds (يَدْخُلُونَ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ أَفْوَاجًا), a community gathering onto the way.
God parts the sea for the Children of Israel, saves them, and drowns Pharaoh's people, a collective passage out of danger.
Safa and Marwa are among God's symbols (شَعَائِرِ اللَّه); pilgrims go between them, leaving a repeated path of seeking and remembrance.
The first House is established for people, blessed and a guidance for all worlds (هُدًى لِّلْعَالَمِينَ), the home toward which the path leads.
The House contains clear signs and Abraham's station; pilgrimage to it is due for those able, completing the route to a known destination.
Moses recalls God's favor (نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ) in appointing prophets, making kings, and giving blessings, before the community is told to enter the land.
Moses commands his people to enter the holy land God assigned them and not turn back, a direct route offered to a favored community.
The people refuse the land because powerful inhabitants are there, turning away from the route through fear.
Two God-fearing men urge the people to enter through the gate and rely on God, a guide's counsel at the threshold.
The people refuse to enter and tell Moses and God to go fight alone, choosing separation from the offered way.
Moses says he controls only himself and his brother and asks God to separate them from the defiantly disobedient, the fracture of a community.
The land is forbidden to them for forty years as they wander through the earth (يَتِيهُونَ فِي الْأَرْض), the explicit consequence of losing the route.
God makes the Sacred House a standing support for people and a place of safety, alongside the sacred months and offerings.
The Children of Israel cross the sea while Pharaoh and his forces pursue; drowning catches him as he claims belief too late.
Pharaoh is told that his belief comes only now after prior rebellion and corruption, when the route of return has closed.
Pharaoh's body is preserved as a sign for later people, a trace left on the road of history.
God takes His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque to show him signs, a guided journey between sanctuaries.
Moses follows the knowledgeable servant by ship; the servant damages it, beginning the next stage of a journey whose sign Moses cannot yet read.
The servant reminds Moses that he said he could not remain patient, testing the traveler's commitment to follow.
Moses asks not to be taken to task for forgetfulness, continuing the learner's effort to stay on the route.
They travel onward and meet a boy whom the servant kills, an act whose meaning remains hidden from the companion.
The servant again recalls his warning about Moses's patience, marking another boundary in the following.
Moses promises that if he asks again, the servant may leave him, accepting the consequences of failing to follow.
They reach a town whose people refuse hospitality; the servant repairs a collapsing wall, the third sign encountered on the road.
The servant announces their parting and promises to explain what Moses could not patiently witness.
The damaged ship belongs to poor people who work at sea; the mark protects their livelihood from a king seizing every sound vessel.
The boy's parents are believers, and the servant fears the boy would drive them into rebellion and disbelief.
God intends to replace the boy with one better in purity and nearer in affection, preserving the parents' way.
The repaired wall belongs to two orphans and hides their treasure; their righteous father and God's mercy preserve their inheritance until they mature.
The Prophet is asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn, introducing another traveler whose route and signs unfold in the passage.
God establishes Dhu al-Qarnayn in the land and gives him a means (سَبَبًا) to every matter, equipping a traveler to follow routes.
Dhu al-Qarnayn follows a means (فَأَتْبَعَ سَبَبًا), the repeated image of taking a way toward each destination.
He reaches the setting of the sun and encounters a people there, a marked limit of his westward journey.
He is told to punish the wrongdoer or treat the believer well, a judgment encountered at the edge of the route.
The believer who does right receives the best reward and an easy command, a fitting course for those who accept guidance.
Dhu al-Qarnayn follows another means (ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَبًا), continuing from one direction to the next.
He reaches the rising of the sun and finds a people with no shelter from it, another distinct region on the journey.
God encompasses all that is with the traveler in knowledge, framing the journey and its people under divine sight.
He follows yet another means (ثُمَّ أَتْبَعَ سَبَبًا), moving toward a third encounter.
He reaches the space between two barriers and finds a people who can barely understand speech, a traveler arriving at a boundary.
The people ask Dhu al-Qarnayn to build a barrier against Gog and Magog, seeking protection for their community.
He asks them to help with strength and offers to build a barrier, making their shared work a defense along the way.
Iron is brought and the gap is filled with molten copper, a physical boundary that stops passage.
Gog and Magog can neither scale nor pierce the barrier, the route held against those who would cross it.
Dhu al-Qarnayn calls the barrier mercy from his Lord and says it will be leveled when God's promise comes, preserving the boundary's temporary nature.
God tells Moses to travel by night with His servants and strike a dry path through the sea (طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا), without fearing pursuit.
Pharaoh pursues them with his forces, then the sea overwhelms him, completing the false leader's route to destruction.
God commands Moses to travel by night with His servants (فَأَسْرِ بِعِبَادِي), beginning the journey out of Pharaoh's rule.
Pharaoh sends gatherers through the cities, mobilizing pursuit behind the travelers.
Pharaoh calls the Children of Israel a small band, dismissing the community fleeing his rule.
He says they have provoked his anger, naming the hostility behind the pursuit.
Pharaoh's forces are described as numerous and alert, the threat following the travelers.
The pursuers leave gardens and springs behind, the settled abundance they will lose.
They leave fields, noble dwellings, and comforts, a trace of what the failed route abandons.
God gives these places to another people, the destination and inheritance of the exodus.
Pharaoh's forces catch up at sunrise, closing the distance on the travelers.
The two groups see one another, and Moses's companions say they have been overtaken.
The pursuing army is brought near the sea, following the same way into its end.
Moses and all who are with him are saved, the guide and his community brought through.
The pursuing others are drowned, the contrary end of the path they chose.
This passage is made a sign, though most people do not believe, leaving a marker for later readers.
God appoints the House for Abraham and commands its purification for those who circle, stand, bow, and prostrate, defining the destination's practices.
Abraham is commanded to call people to pilgrimage; they come on foot and on lean camels from every deep pass (كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ), converging from distant roads.
Pilgrims witness benefits and remember God's name over the cattle He provides, joining the journey to gratitude.
Pilgrims fulfill vows, end their rites, and circle the Ancient House, completing the route to its home.
